title: Joshua 11:1–15
context: After the southern campaign of chapter 10, Jabin king of Hazor gathers a large northern coalition at the waters of Merom. The LORD tells Joshua not to fear and commands him to hamstring the enemy’s horses and burn their chariots. Israel wins, pursues the fleeing armies, captures Hazor, and devotes its people to destruction, burning that city alone. This devoting to destruction, called herem, was a specific command given in Israel’s unique covenant-historical setting. It was tied to God’s judgment on the wickedness and idolatry of Canaan (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5; 20:16–18). It is presented as the LORD’s judgment carried out through Israel, not as a pattern for later generations. The text is stark, and the notes do not soften it. Both traditions read it soberly, and both deny that it licenses violence against any people today. The section closes by stressing Joshua’s complete obedience to what the LORD commanded through Moses.

verses.text: When Jabin king of Hazor heard of it, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, to the king of Shimron, to the king of Achshaph,
verses.arminianNotes:
Jabin king of Hazor hears of Israel’s victories and sends to the kings of Madon, Shimron, and Achshaph. Judges 4:2 later mentions another Jabin king of Hazor, which interpreters explain in different ways, such as a dynastic name.

Arminian readers note that the kings respond to news of what God has done by choosing to resist rather than to seek peace, as Gibeon did.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that opposition to God’s people often grows in proportion to God’s visible work among them. Hazor’s king takes the lead because he sees a threat to his dominion.

Both traditions read the coalition as human pride organizing itself against the LORD’s purposes.

verses.text: and to the kings who were on the north, in the hill country, in the Arabah south of Chinneroth, in the lowland, and in the heights of Dor on the west,
verses.arminianNotes:
The summons goes to kings in the north, the hill country, the Arabah south of Chinneroth, the lowland, and the heights of Dor. The coalition covers a wide region.

Arminian readers note that the size of the alliance reflects the scale of the decision these rulers made: a unified rejection of Israel’s God rather than individual surrender.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the comprehensive geography: the whole north rises together, so that the victory will display the LORD’s power over the entire land.

Both traditions avoid speculating on the exact location of every region named and focus on the breadth of the opposition.

verses.text: to the Canaanite on the east and on the west, the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite in the hill country, and the Hivite under Hermon in the land of Mizpah.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Canaanites east and west, the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, and Hivites under Hermon join the alliance. Most of these peoples are named in God’s promises to give the land (compare Genesis 15:19–21; Exodus 3:8).

Arminian readers note that these nations had long occupied the land, and that their judgment came only after an extended period of divine patience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the very peoples God named to Abraham now gather in one place. History is moving toward the fulfillment of his word.

Both traditions see here God’s promise to Abraham, spoken centuries earlier, reaching its appointed time.

verses.text: They went out, they and all their armies with them, many people, even as the sand that is on the seashore in multitude, with very many horses and chariots.
verses.arminianNotes:
The armies come out with many people, as numerous as the sand on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots. Israel faces overwhelming odds.

Arminian readers note that the image of sand on the seashore echoes God’s promise to Abraham’s offspring, now ironically applied to Israel’s enemies. Faith must trust God against visible strength.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God often allows his people to face impossible odds so that victory is clearly his. Chariots were the most advanced military power of the time.

Both traditions see the scene as a test of whether Israel would trust the LORD or fear human might (compare Psalm 20:7).

verses.text: All these kings met together; and they came and encamped together at the waters of Merom, to fight with Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
All these kings meet and encamp at the waters of Merom to fight Israel. The location of Merom is uncertain.

Arminian readers note that the kings make a deliberate, coordinated decision to fight, a choice for which they bear responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the gathering of the enemy in one place, which looked like a threat, became the occasion of a single decisive victory. God governs the movements of armies.

Both traditions treat the identification of Merom cautiously and focus on the confrontation between the coalition and the LORD’s people.

verses.text: The LORD said to Joshua, “Don’t be afraid because of them; for tomorrow at this time, I will deliver them up all slain before Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Joshua not to be afraid, promises to deliver the enemy by tomorrow, and commands him to hamstring their horses and burn their chariots. The promise comes before the battle.

Arminian readers note that God’s word invites Joshua’s trust and obedience; faith acts on promise before seeing results.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the command to destroy the chariots keeps Israel from trusting in military power (compare Deuteronomy 17:16). God wants his people to rely on him.

Both traditions hear the repeated command not to fear (compare Joshua 1:9; 10:8) as grace that strengthens obedience.

verses.text: So Joshua came suddenly, with all the warriors, against them by the waters of Merom, and attacked them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua comes suddenly with all his warriors and attacks the enemy at the waters of Merom. He acts promptly.

Arminian readers note that Joshua’s swift action shows faith responding to God’s promise. Divine assurance does not make human action unnecessary; it empowers it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s promise and Joshua’s action fit together: God ordains both the end and the means. Joshua’s boldness is the fruit of God’s word.

Both traditions agree that God’s sovereignty and human obedience work together here rather than competing with each other.

verses.text: The LORD delivered them into the hand of Israel, and they struck them, and chased them to great Sidon, and to Misrephoth Maim, and to the valley of Mizpah eastward. They struck them until they left them no one remaining.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD delivers the enemy into Israel’s hand, and Israel pursues them to Sidon, Misrephoth Maim, and the valley of Mizpah, leaving none remaining. The victory is attributed first to God.

Arminian readers note that Israel fights, yet the decisive act is the LORD’s. Human effort is real but dependent on divine help.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the order of the sentence places God’s act before Israel’s pursuit. The battle belongs to the LORD.

Both traditions read the victory as God’s faithfulness to his promise, while treating the text’s violence soberly within its unique covenant setting.

verses.text: Joshua did to them as the LORD told him. He hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua does as the LORD told him, hamstringing the horses and burning the chariots. Obedience is precise.

Arminian readers note that Joshua could have kept the chariots as valuable assets, but he chose to obey. Faithfulness sometimes requires giving up what seems useful.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Israel’s strength was not to be in horses and chariots but in the LORD. The destruction of the chariots is an act of trust (compare Psalm 20:7).

Both traditions see a lasting principle: God’s people must not rely on the instruments of power that the world trusts.

verses.text: Joshua turned back at that time, and took Hazor, and struck its king with the sword; for Hazor used to be the head of all those kingdoms.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua turns back and takes Hazor, striking its king, for Hazor had been the head of all those kingdoms. The leading city falls.

Arminian readers note that the fall of the coalition’s leader reflects the consequences of the choice Jabin made in organizing resistance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God brings down the proud city that claimed leadership over the region (compare Luke 1:52). Hazor is generally identified with a large mound north of the Sea of Galilee.

Both traditions treat archaeological questions cautiously and focus on the text’s theological point.

verses.text: They struck all the souls who were in it with the edge of the sword, utterly destroying them. There was no one left who breathed. He burned Hazor with fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel strikes everyone in Hazor, devoting them to destruction, leaving no one who breathed, and burns the city. This is herem.

Arminian readers acknowledge the starkness of this verse and read it as a unique act of judgment on Canaanite wickedness (compare Deuteronomy 9:4–5), not a pattern for later conduct.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read it within God’s judgment in this specific redemptive-historical moment, tied to the iniquity of the Amorites reaching its full measure (Genesis 15:16).

Both traditions refuse to sanitize the text, and both deny that it licenses violence against any people today.

verses.text: Joshua captured all the cities of those kings, with their kings, and he struck them with the edge of the sword, and utterly destroyed them, as Moses the servant of the LORD commanded.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua captures all the cities of those kings and devotes them to destruction, as Moses commanded. The command came from Deuteronomy 20:16–18.

Arminian readers note that the stated reason for the command was to keep Israel from learning the detestable practices of the nations, including idolatry and child sacrifice (compare Deuteronomy 12:31).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Joshua’s conduct is measured by its faithfulness to God’s word through Moses. The narrative presents obedience, not personal ambition.

Both traditions read the command as unique to Israel’s entry into the land, not as a model for the church, whose warfare is spiritual (2 Corinthians 10:3–5).

verses.text: But as for the cities that stood on their mounds, Israel burned none of them, except Hazor only. Joshua burned that.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel burned none of the cities standing on their mounds except Hazor. Most cities were preserved.

Arminian readers note that God gave Israel cities they did not build (compare Deuteronomy 6:10–11), a gift calling for gratitude and faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the preservation of the cities shows God’s purpose to give Israel a land to dwell in, not merely to destroy. Hazor’s burning was a particular judgment.

Both traditions see the distinction as evidence that the campaign had specific limits set by God’s command.

verses.text: The children of Israel took all the plunder of these cities, with the livestock, as plunder for themselves; but every man they struck with the edge of the sword, until they had destroyed them. They didn’t leave any who breathed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel takes the plunder and livestock but strikes every person, leaving none who breathed. Unlike Jericho, the plunder is permitted.

Arminian readers note the difference from Jericho (Joshua 6:18–19), where all was devoted to God, and from Ai, where plunder was allowed (Joshua 8:2).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God sets the terms for each situation; what he forbade at Jericho, he allowed here. Obedience means following his specific word.

Both traditions read the verse with sobriety and hold that its herem language belongs to this unique moment, not to any later practice.

verses.text: As the LORD commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua. Joshua did so. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD commanded Moses.
verses.arminianNotes:
As the LORD commanded Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua, and Joshua left nothing undone. The chain of obedience is emphasized.

Arminian readers note that Joshua’s faithfulness is genuinely his own, and Scripture commends him for it. Obedience is a real response to God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the chain runs from the LORD through Moses to Joshua, showing that God’s word governs the whole process. Joshua is a faithful servant.

Both traditions see Joshua as a model of wholehearted obedience, and they read this verse in contrast to Israel’s later failures in Judges.
